How Much Land Does a Man Need? Leo Tolstoy's How Much Land Does a Man Need? is a folk parable about insatiable greed told with devastating simplicity. Pahom is a poor peasant who dreams of owning land and believes that if only he had sufficient acreage, he would never want for anything and could live in comfort. He acquires some land through hard work but, dissatisfied, learns of the Bashkirs, a distant people who supposedly offer vast tracts of land for a pittance. The Bashkir elder offers him a bargain: any land he can circumscribe on foot in a single day is his, for a small fee. Pahom begins walking at dawn, driven by the magnitude of possibility, striding farther and farther across the steppe as the sun descends. As evening approaches and he realizes he has overextended himself, he runs desperately back to the starting point to complete the circuit before sundown. He collapses upon reaching his destination, dead from exertion, having claimed vast acreage that he will never possess or enjoy. His servant buries him in a six-foot plot of earth, answering the story's title question with grim irony. The tale is structured as a moral fable, a definitive statement on the destructiveness of unlimited ambition that traces the arc of human desire and its inevitable terminus.
